Lessons.Title: Rational and Irrational Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: classify numbers obtained from quadratic-equation solutions as rational or irrational, and explain how a perfect-square discriminant affects the type of roots when integer coefficients are used. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 20 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/20/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/20/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source revisits Grade 8 number classifications and roots rather than claiming every quadratic has irrational roots.

Original comparison: x²−5x+6=0=(x−2)(x−3) gives two rational roots2 and3. x²−2=0 yields ±√2, both irrational. x²−2x−1=0 has discriminant4+4=8, and roots (2±√8)/2=1±√2, irrational. An irrational root remains a real number.

A rational number is expressible as p/q with integers p,q and q≠0; integers and finite/recurring decimals qualify. Irrational numbers do not have such a rational representation. For an integer-coefficient quadratic with D≥0, a perfect-square integer D produces rational formula roots; non-square positive integer D produces irrational roots when the radical part cannot cancel with rational coefficient.

Student task: sort radical expressions and rational decimals, verify root classifications from exact equations, estimate locations, and critique the claim that √16 is irrational merely because it is written with a radical. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for correct classification, mathematical evidence, valid root derivation and explanations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rational number
KeyConcepts.Definition: A number p/q for integers q≠0, including integers and terminating or repeating decimals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Irrational number
KeyConcepts.Definition: A real number not equal to any ratio of integers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discriminant type
KeyConcepts.Definition: For integer coefficients, an exact positive non-square integer D typically gives irrational roots through formula.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming any written square root is irrational

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Irrational numbers lie on real line.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replacing exact radical with rounded decimal to classify rationality
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A finite approximation can disguise an irrational value.

SummaryPoints: Real roots can be rational or irrational.
Perfect-square roots are rational even when written as radicals.
x²−2 and x²−2x−1 have irrational real roots.
Teacher reviews exact forms and number classifications.
